T5A01: Current, the rate of electron flow, is measured in amperes (amps). Volts measure electrical pressure (voltage), watts measure power, and ohms measure resistance.
T5A02: Power, the rate at which energy is used, is measured in watts. Watt-hours measure energy (power × time), which is what your electric bill charges for.
T5A03: Current is the term for the flow of electrons in a circuit. Voltage is the 'push' that causes current to flow. Analogy: voltage is water pressure; current is the amount of water flowing.
T5A04: Frequency is the number of complete cycles per second of an alternating current or wave. It is measured in hertz (Hz).
T5A05: Electrons flow because of a difference in voltage (electrical potential) between two points. Without a voltage difference, there's no push and no current.
T5A06: Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz), meaning cycles per second. The henry is the unit of inductance and the farad is the unit of capacitance.
T5A07: Metals conduct well because they have many free electrons that can easily move through the material when a voltage is applied.
T5A08: Glass is a good insulator: its electrons are tightly bound and cannot move freely. Sea water (salt water), stainless steel, and graphite all conduct electricity.
T5A09: Alternating current (AC) reverses direction periodically, flowing in a positive direction, then negative, over and over. The answers that describe current alternating between one direction and zero are not AC.
T5A10: Power is the rate at which electrical energy is used (or delivered), measured in watts.
T5A11: Resistance opposes the flow of every kind of current: DC, AC, and RF alike. (Reactance, by contrast, affects only AC.)
T5B01: Milli means one-thousandth, so 1 ampere = 1000 milliamperes. 1.5 A × 1000 = 1500 mA.
T5B02: Kilo = 1,000. 1,500,000 Hz ÷ 1,000 = 1500 kHz (which also equals 1.5 MHz).
T5B03: Kilo means 1,000, so one kilovolt (kV) = 1,000 volts.
T5B04: Micro means one-millionth (10^-6). So one microvolt (µV) = 0.000001 volt.
T5B08: Pico = 10^-12, micro = 10^-6. There are 1,000,000 picofarads in 1 microfarad.
T5B09: Doubling power is an increase of about 3 dB. 5 W to 10 W is double, so +3 dB. Memory tip: ×2 = +3 dB, ×4 = +6 dB, ×10 = +10 dB.
T5B10: 12 W to 3 W is one-quarter of the power. Halving is -3 dB, so halving twice (12 → 6 → 3) is -6 dB.
T5B11: 20 W to 200 W is a 10-fold increase, which is exactly 10 dB (dB = 10 × log10(200/20) = 10 × 1).
T5B12: To convert kHz to MHz, divide by 1000: 28400 kHz = 28.400 MHz (in the 10-meter band).
T5B13: To convert MHz to GHz, divide by 1000: 2425 MHz = 2.425 GHz.
T5C01: Capacitance is the ability to store energy in an electric field (between the plates of a capacitor). Inductance stores energy in a magnetic field.
T5C02: Capacitance is measured in farads (F). Practical capacitors are usually measured in microfarads (µF) or picofarads (pF).
T5C03: Inductance is the ability to store energy in a magnetic field, such as the field around a coil of wire.
T5C04: Inductance is measured in henries (H). The farad is for capacitance; the ohm is for resistance and impedance.
T5C05: Impedance, the total opposition to AC (resistance plus reactance), is measured in ohms, the same unit as resistance.
T5C06: Kilohertz is abbreviated kHz: lowercase 'k' for kilo and 'Hz' for hertz (capital H because it's named after Heinrich Hertz).
T5C07: Megahertz is abbreviated MHz: capital 'M' for mega (lowercase 'm' means milli, a huge difference!) and 'Hz' for hertz.
T5C08: Power (watts) = current (amps) × voltage (volts), P = I × E. E is the symbol for voltage (from 'electromotive force').
T5C09: P = I × E = 10 A × 13.8 V = 138 watts.
T5C10: P = I × E = 2.5 A × 12 V = 30 watts.
T5C11: Rearrange P = I × E to I = P / E. I = 120 W / 12 V = 10 amperes.
T5C12: Impedance is the total opposition to AC current flow. It includes resistance and reactance (from capacitors and inductors).
T5D01: Ohm's Law: current (I) = voltage (E) / resistance (R). Memory aid: cover the quantity you want in the triangle E over I × R.
T5D04: R = E / I = 90 V / 3 A = 30 ohms.
T5D05: R = E / I = 12 V / 1.5 A = 8 ohms.
T5D06: R = E / I = 12 V / 4 A = 3 ohms.
T5D07: I = E / R = 120 V / 80 Ω = 1.5 amperes.
T5D08: I = E / R = 200 V / 100 Ω = 2 amperes.
T5D09: I = E / R = 240 V / 24 Ω = 10 amperes.
T5D10: E = I × R = 0.5 A × 2 Ω = 1 volt.
T5D11: E = I × R = 1 A × 10 Ω = 10 volts.
T5D12: E = I × R = 2 A × 10 Ω = 20 volts.
T5D13: In a series circuit there is only one path, so the same current flows through every component.
T5D14: In a parallel circuit every component is connected across the same two points, so each one has the same voltage across it.
T6A01: A resistor opposes (resists) the flow of current in a circuit, including DC. An inductor opposes changes in current, but has little effect on steady DC.
T6A02: A potentiometer is a variable resistor with a sliding contact. It's the classic volume control knob.
T6A03: A potentiometer controls resistance: turning the knob moves a wiper along a resistive element.
T6A04: A capacitor stores energy in an electric field between its plates.
T6A05: A capacitor is made of conductive surfaces (plates) separated by an insulator (dielectric).
T6A06: An inductor stores energy in a magnetic field.
T6A07: An inductor is typically a coil of wire. Coiling the wire concentrates the magnetic field, increasing inductance.
T6A08: SPDT = Single Pole, Double Throw. One circuit (single pole) can be switched to either of two other circuits (double throw). Like a light switch at the top and bottom of a stairway.
T6A09: Component 3 in figure T-2 is a simple on/off switch: a single lever that either connects or breaks one path. That is a single-pole single-throw (SPST) switch.
T6A10: Nickel-metal hydride (NiMH), lithium-ion, and lead-acid batteries are all rechargeable chemistries.
T6A11: Carbon-zinc batteries (the old-style 'heavy duty' cells) are not rechargeable. NiCd, lead-acid, and Li-ion are all rechargeable.
T6B01: Forward voltage drop varies by diode type. For example, a silicon diode drops about 0.7 V, a germanium or Schottky diode only about 0.2-0.3 V. That drop does reduce the voltage delivered to the load, and it's normal.
T6B02: A diode allows current to flow in only one direction, from anode to cathode. That's why diodes are used in rectifiers to change AC into DC.
T6B03: A transistor can act as an electronic switch. A small current or voltage at the base or gate turns a larger current on or off.
T6B04: A bipolar transistor is made of three regions of semiconductor material (NPN or PNP). Triodes and pentodes are vacuum tubes.
T6B05: Field-effect transistors (FETs) have gate, drain, and source terminals. Bipolar junction transistors have emitter, base, and collector.
T6B06: The cathode end of a diode is usually marked with a stripe (band). This matches the bar in the diode schematic symbol.
T6B07: An LED emits light when forward current flows through it. Reverse-biased, it stays dark.
T6B08: FET stands for Field Effect Transistor, a transistor in which an electric field (set by the gate voltage) controls current flow.
T6B09: A diode's two electrodes are the anode and the cathode. Current flows from anode to cathode.
T6B10: A transistor can provide power gain: a small input signal controls a larger output signal. A transformer can step voltage up but not add power.
T6B11: Gain describes how much an amplifier increases a signal: output voltage relative to input voltage, output current relative to input current, or output power relative to input power. All are valid uses.
T6B12: A bipolar junction transistor (BJT) has an emitter, a base, and a collector.
T6C01: A diagram using standard component symbols is a schematic. It shows how components are connected, not their physical layout.
T6C02: Component 1 in figure T-1 is the zigzag line, which is the symbol for a resistor.
T6C03: Component 2 in figure T-1 is a circle with a bar and two lines, one with an arrow (the emitter). That's a bipolar junction transistor (NPN).
T6C04: Component 3 in figure T-1 is a lamp, shown as a bulb outline with a filament inside.
T6C05: Component 4 in figure T-1, the alternating long and short parallel lines, is a battery. The long line is the positive terminal.
T6C06: Component 6 in figure T-2 is two plates (one straight, one curved) with a gap. That's a capacitor (here, a filter capacitor in a power supply).
T6C07: Component 8 in figure T-2 is a diode symbol with arrows pointing outward, showing light being emitted. That's a light emitting diode (LED).
T6C08: Component 9 in figure T-2 is a resistor (zigzag) with an arrow touching it: a variable resistor (potentiometer or rheostat).
T6C09: Component 4 in figure T-2 is two coils side by side with lines between them (the iron core). That's a transformer.
T6C10: Component 3 in figure T-3 is a coil (inductor) with an arrow touching it, meaning it is a variable inductor. Figure T-3 shows an antenna tuner.
T6C11: Component 4 in figure T-3, the triangle-like shape at the top, is the antenna symbol.
T6C12: Schematics accurately show how components are connected to each other. They do not show wire lengths or what components physically look like.
T6D01: A rectifier converts alternating current into a varying (pulsating) direct current, typically using diodes. Filtering then smooths it into steady DC.
T6D02: A relay is an electrically controlled switch: current through a coil creates a magnetic field that moves the switch contacts.
T6D03: Shielded wire has a conductive covering that prevents unwanted signals from coupling into or radiating out of the wire. That reduces interference.
T6D04: A meter displays an electrical quantity (such as voltage, current, or power) as a numeric value.
T6D05: A regulator controls (holds steady) the output voltage of a power supply despite changes in load or input voltage.
T6D06: A transformer changes AC voltage from one level to another, for example stepping 120 V AC household power down to a lower voltage.
T6D07: An LED (light emitting diode) is commonly used as a visual indicator, such as a power or transmit light. FETs and Zener diodes don't emit light.
T6D08: An inductor combined with a capacitor forms a resonant (tuned) circuit that responds strongly at one particular frequency.
T6D09: An integrated circuit (IC) combines many transistors, diodes, resistors and other components into a single package (chip).
T6D10: Component 2 in figure T-1 is a transistor. In this circuit it acts as a switch/amplifier to control the flow of current through the lamp.
T6D11: A resonant (tuned) circuit is an inductor and a capacitor connected in series or parallel. It resonates at the frequency where their reactances are equal.
